name: PPIB (HERDA)
summary: PPIB encodes cyclophilin B, an enzyme that helps fold and process collagen. A missense change in exon 1, c.115G>A (p.Gly39Arg; g.129307092G>A on chromosome 1, EquCab3.0), impairs that and causes hereditary equine regional dermal asthenia (HERDA): fragile, over-stretchy skin that tears and scars. It is recessive; carriers are normally healthy. Signs in a horse with two copies usually appear at about a year and a half to two years old. The disease as documented is of the skin; the bone disease that PPIB mutations cause in people is not the picture in horses. Found in the American Quarter Horse and breeds with Quarter Horse ancestry, including Paint Horses and Appaloosas, and far commoner in cutting and cow-horse lines. Laboratories usually write the genotypes N/N, N/HR and HR/HR; UC Davis writes N/HRD for a carrier. No effect on coat, height, speed or build is established.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: Two working copies. Nothing is wrong and nothing is passed on.

phenotypes.name: PPIB (HERDA) carrier
phenotypes.description: One copy. Typically healthy, with nothing to see; the horse passes the copy to half its foals. A foal is affected only when both parents pass it on.

phenotypes.name: HERDA (fragile skin)
phenotypes.description: Two copies. The skin is loose, thin, over-stretchy and poorly attached to the tissue beneath. Minor knocks, above all along the back, withers and saddle area, split it open, with fluid swellings, wounds that heal slowly and scarring. Signs usually appear at about a year and a half to two years old. The horse lives, but often cannot tolerate tack, which limits riding and showing.

American Quarter Horse in the United States (7 carriers in 200 control horses, 3.5%, Tryon et al. 2007; an earlier estimate gave 3.65% of 1,041 unaffected horses; the share of affected horses is not given)
Quarter Horse in France (1.6% carriers, Veterinary Dermatology 2011; the share of affected horses is not given)
American Quarter Horse, elite cutting horses (32 carriers in 113, 28.3%, Tryon et al. 2009; allele frequency 0.142; a high-risk subgroup, not the breed)
